subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which factor best explains the persistence of core-periphery patterns at a global scale?
options: Unequal terms of trade, debt and concentration of high-value activity in the core
questions.explain: Structural inequalities in trade, debt burdens and the location of profitable activity reinforce core dominance over the periphery.

questions.q: A major criticism of Rostow's model is that it:
options: Is Eurocentric and assumes all countries follow the same Western path
questions.explain: Critics argue the model wrongly universalises the Western experience and ignores colonial and global structural barriers.

questions.q: Why can a country have a high GNI per capita but a low HDI?
options: Wealth may be unevenly invested, leaving health and education indicators weak
questions.explain: Resource-rich states can have high average income yet poor schooling and life expectancy if wealth is not invested in people.

questions.q: Which best describes 'top-down' versus 'bottom-up' development strategies?
options: Top-down is large-scale, externally led; bottom-up is small-scale, community-led
questions.explain: Top-down projects are big, state/donor-driven schemes, while bottom-up approaches empower local communities with appropriate technology.

questions.q: What is the epidemiological (health) transition?
options: A change from manual to automated farming
A shift from communicable to non-communicable diseases as a country develops
The spread of a single pandemic globally
A move from rural to urban living
questions.explain: As development raises life expectancy, the main disease burden shifts from infectious to chronic, lifestyle-related conditions.

questions.q: What is the central argument of Frank's dependency theory?
options: Population growth is the main barrier to development
All countries develop through identical stages
Free trade automatically closes the development gap
Underdevelopment is caused by the core's exploitation of the periphery
questions.explain: Dependency theory argues poorer peripheral nations are kept underdeveloped by exploitation from wealthy core nations.

questions.q: What role do IGOs such as the UN play in advancing development and rights?
options: They set norms, coordinate aid and peacekeeping, and monitor rights globally
questions.explain: IGOs establish international standards, channel assistance and monitor compliance, though their power depends on member states.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'development gap'?
options: The widening difference in living standards between the richest and poorest
The time lag before a census is published
A shortfall in a government's annual budget
The difference between GDP and GNI
questions.explain: The development gap describes the disparity in wealth and quality of life between the most and least developed nations.

questions.q: Which IGO is primarily responsible for global health coordination?
questions.explain: The WHO directs and coordinates international health within the UN system.

questions.q: What is a key criticism of military or aid interventions intended to advance human rights?
options: They can mask geopolitical or economic self-interest and undermine sovereignty
questions.explain: Interventions are often criticised for serving the intervening state's strategic interests and eroding national sovereignty.

questions.q: Rostow's modernisation model is best described as a theory of what?
questions.explain: Rostow's model proposes that countries progress through five sequential stages of growth towards mass consumption.

questions.q: Which of these is a communicable disease?
questions.explain: Malaria is transmitted by mosquito vector and is therefore communicable, unlike the chronic non-communicable examples.

questions.q: The Gender Inequality Index (GII) reflects disadvantage in which three dimensions?
options: Reproductive health, empowerment and labour market
questions.explain: The GII combines reproductive health, empowerment (parliamentary seats and education) and labour-market participation.

questions.q: In Rostow's final stage, 'high mass consumption', the economy is dominated by what?
options: A large service sector and widespread consumer durables
questions.explain: At high mass consumption, output and employment shift to services and consumers can purchase abundant durable goods.

questions.q: What three dimensions does the Human Development Index (HDI) combine?
questions.explain: The HDI is a composite of GNI per capita (income), schooling (education) and life expectancy (health).

questions.q: How can globalisation widen the development gap?
options: Through unequal flows that concentrate profit and skilled jobs in core economies
By guaranteeing equal trade terms for all
questions.explain: Globalisation can entrench inequality when TNC profits, investment and high-value work concentrate in already-wealthy regions.

questions.q: The Social Progress Index is notable because it deliberately excludes which variable?
questions.explain: The Social Progress Index measures social and environmental outcomes without using economic indicators, complementing GDP.

questions.q: What is 'remittance' income and why does it matter for development?
options: Interest on national debt; it harms development
Money migrants send home; it can exceed aid and boost local economies
Profit repatriated by TNCs; it reduces incomes
Government foreign aid; it is unimportant
questions.explain: Remittances are earnings migrants send to families, often surpassing official aid and supporting consumption and investment.

questions.q: Why is gender equality considered central to development?
options: Empowering women raises education, health, productivity and reduces poverty
It only matters in high-income countries
questions.explain: Educating and empowering women improves household welfare, child outcomes and economic growth, accelerating development.

questions.q: How does poor health act as both a cause and consequence of underdevelopment?
options: Illness reduces productivity and incomes, while poverty limits access to healthcare
questions.explain: Disease lowers workforce productivity and earnings, and low incomes in turn restrict access to treatment, creating a cycle.

questions.q: Which limitation most undermines GDP as a development measure?
options: It cannot be calculated for large economies
It says nothing about distribution, informal activity or wellbeing
questions.explain: GDP ignores income distribution, much informal activity and quality-of-life factors, so high GDP can mask deprivation.

questions.q: What does the Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI) measure that income-based poverty lines do not?
options: Overlapping deprivations in health, education and living standards
questions.explain: The MPI captures simultaneous deprivations across health, education and living standards rather than just income.

questions.q: How might trade rather than aid promote long-term development?
options: It builds sustainable income, industry and capacity within recipient economies
questions.explain: Fairer trade access can generate self-sustaining incomes and industrial capacity, unlike aid which can foster dependency.

questions.q: Which is a non-communicable disease (NCD)?
questions.explain: Cardiovascular disease is non-infectious and linked to lifestyle and ageing, unlike the communicable alternatives.

questions.q: In Wallerstein's world-systems theory, which category sits between core and periphery?
questions.explain: Wallerstein added a semi-periphery of intermediate, industrialising states between the dominant core and exploited periphery.

questions.q: What does it mean that human rights have a distinct 'geography'?
options: Rights only apply at the equator
Protection and abuse of rights vary significantly between and within countries
questions.explain: The degree to which rights are upheld differs spatially, shaped by political, cultural and economic context.

questions.q: What does the Gini coefficient measure?
options: Income or wealth inequality within a population
questions.explain: The Gini coefficient quantifies inequality, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (maximum inequality).

questions.q: In Rostow's model, the 'take-off' stage is characterised by what?
options: Rapid industrialisation and rising investment in key sectors
questions.explain: Take-off involves a surge in manufacturing and investment that drives sustained, self-reinforcing growth.

questions.q: Why is GNI per capita (PPP) often preferred to GDP for comparing living standards between countries?
options: It excludes the informal economy entirely
It adjusts for differences in the cost of living and includes income from abroad
questions.explain: GNI counts income earned abroad, and PPP adjustment corrects for differing price levels so values are more comparable.

questions.q: Which UN measure underpins the international framework for human rights?
options: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)
questions.explain: The 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights sets out the foundational global standard for human rights.
